summary.case_overview: Writ Petition (Civil) 135 of 1970 was filed by Kesavananda Bharati against the State of Kerala, challenging the constitutional validity of the Kerala Land Reforms Act as amended, along with the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments to the Constitution of India [Page 1] [Page 2]. A 13-judge Bench of the Supreme Court heard the matter to determine the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, the correct interpretation of Article 13(2), the validity of the impugned constitutional amendments, and whether the earlier decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was correctly decided [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 501].
summary.facts_of_case: The petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 on March 21, 1970 under Article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31, seeking to declare the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (as amended by Act 35 of 1969) unconstitutional and void [Page 1]. During the pendency of the petition, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 was passed [Page 1]. Subsequently, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act [Page 2]. The Twenty-ninth Amendment placed the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Acts of 1969 and 1971 into the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution [Page 2]. The Supreme Court granted the petitioner permission to amend the writ petition to challenge these constitutional amendments [Page 2]. The Constitution Bench then referred the case to a larger 13-judge bench to determine the extent of the amending power under Article 368 and whether I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was correctly decided [Page 2].
summary.legal_issues:
1. What is the extent and scope of the power conferred on Parliament to amend the Constitution under Article 368 [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 309]?
2. Was I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab correctly decided in holding that fundamental rights cannot be abridged or taken away by a constitutional amendment and that a constitutional amendment is 'law' under Article 13(2) [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 484] [Page 501]?
3. Are there inherent or implied limitations on the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution under Article 368 [Page 6] [Page 91] [Page 487] [Page 501]?
4. Are the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 129] [Page 194] [Page 374] [Page 501]?
summary.important_arguments_or_content:
The respondents submitted that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is unlimited and enables Parliament to abrogate fundamental rights, alter the democratic structure, or set up any form of government short of repealing the entire Constitution [Page 2]. They contended that no implied or inherent limitations exist on the amending power, that Article 368 contains both power and procedure, and that constitutional amendments do not constitute 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) [Page 91] [Page 104] [Page 485].

The petitioners submitted that the amending power of Parliament under Article 368 is limited and subject to inherent and implied limitations derived from the scheme of the Constitution, its Preamble, and essential features [Page 2] [Page 91] [Page 487]. They argued that Parliament cannot alter or destroy the basic structure, essential features, or identity of the Constitution, nor can it abrogate fundamental rights guaranteed to citizens [Page 2] [Page 91] [Page 258] [Page 487-488]. They specifically contended that Article 31C subverts fundamental rights and destroys the supreme authority of the Constitution by delegating amending power [Page 2] [Page 245] [Page 496].
summary.court_reasoning:
The Court considered the nature of constituent power versus ordinary legislative power, holding that Article 368 contains both the power and procedure to amend the Constitution and that a constitutional amendment is an exercise of constituent power, not ordinary law-making under Articles 245, 246, or 248 [Page 7] [Page 129] [Page 309] [Page 486] [Page 501]. Consequently, constitutional amendments do not fall within the prohibition of 'law' under Article 13(2) [Page 3] [Page 129] [Page 485] [Page 501].

Regarding the extent of the amending power, Sikri C.J., Hegde J., Khanna J., and other members of the Bench observed that while Article 368 confers broad power to amend any provision of the Constitution, this power does not extend to abrogating, damaging, or destroying the basic structure, essential elements, or framework of the Constitution [Page 104] [Page 258] [Page 374]. Khanna J. reasoned that the second part of Article 31C, which barred judicial review of whether a law actually gives effect to the policy under Article 39(b) or (c), struck at the basic structure of the Constitution and was invalid [Page 374]. Other judges (such as Ray, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, and Chandrachud JJ.) took the view that there are no inherent limitations on the amending power and that every provision of the Constitution can be amended [Page 181] [Page 488] [Page 501].

Regarding the 24th Amendment, the Court held it valid as it merely clarified that Parliament exercises constituent power under Article 368 to amend any provision and that Article 13 does not apply to such amendments [Page 129] [Page 374] [Page 494] [Page 501]. Regarding Section 2 of the 25th Amendment, the substitution of 'amount' for 'compensation' removed the requirement of providing a market value 'just equivalent', but courts retain jurisdiction to review whether the amount fixed is illusory or arbitrary, or if the law is a fraud on the Constitution [Page 194] [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 498] [Page 501]. Regarding Article 31C, courts retain jurisdiction to check whether a law has a direct and reasonable nexus to securing the objectives in Article 39(b) or (c) [Page 425] [Page 498] [Page 501-502]. The 29th Amendment was held valid as placing statutes in the Ninth Schedule provides immunity under Article 31B [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 501].
summary.decision_or_conclusion:
1. The majority overruled I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab, holding that Article 368 contains both power and procedure to amend the Constitution, and that a constitutional amendment is not 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) [Page 6] [Page 309] [Page 501].
2. The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 was held to be valid [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 494] [Page 501].
3. Section 2(a) and 2(b) of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 were held to be valid [Page 258] [Page 361] [Page 495] [Page 501].
4. Section 3 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 (introducing Article 31C) was declared valid to the extent that it protects laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c), but the declaration clause barring judicial review ('and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy') was declared unconstitutional and severed [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501-502]. Courts retain jurisdiction to examine if a direct and reasonable nexus exists between the law and Article 39(b) or (c) [Page 425] [Page 501-502].
5. The Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 was declared valid [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 500] [Page 501].
6. The Supreme Court ordered that the writ petitions be remitted to a Constitution Bench for determination and disposal in accordance with law [Page 502].

summary.simplified_explanation:
Kesavananda Bharati, the head of a religious institution in Kerala, challenged state land reform laws that restricted his property rights [Page 1]. While his case was pending, Parliament passed three major constitutional amendments (the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments) to protect land reform laws and give Parliament power to alter fundamental rights [Page 1] [Page 2]. 

A special 13-judge Bench of the Supreme Court evaluated how far Parliament's power to alter the Constitution goes [Page 1] [Page 2]. The Court held that Parliament has the power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, overruling an earlier case called Golak Nath [Page 6] [Page 309] [Page 501]. However, the Court decided that Parliament cannot alter, damage, or destroy the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution [Page 104] [Page 258] [Page 374]. 

The Court upheld the 24th and 29th Amendments [Page 129] [Page 374] [Page 501]. It also upheld parts of the 25th Amendment allowing the government to pay an 'amount' instead of full market compensation for acquired property, but struck down the portion of Article 31C that barred courts from checking whether a law actually served the public welfare goals under the Directive Principles [Page 194] [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 501-502].
